passages.t: At a ruler's table, and wealth that flies away
passages.happening:
‘When you sit down to dine with a ruler, consider carefully what is set before you’ (verse 1). Restrain a big appetite. ‘Do not crave his delicacies, for that food is deceptive’ (verse 3).

‘Do not wear yourself out to get rich; be wise enough to restrain yourself’ (verse 4). “When you glance at wealth, it disappears, for it makes wings for itself and flies like an eagle to the sky” (verse 5).

Do not eat with a stingy host, who tells you to eat and drink while he counts the cost, and whose heart is not with you (verses 6-7). ‘Do not speak to a fool, for he will despise the wisdom of your words’ (verse 9).

‘Do not move an ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless, for their Redeemer is strong; He will take up their case against you’ (verses 10-11). ‘Apply your heart to instruction and your ears to words of knowledge’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
These are more of the Words of the Wise, mostly commands with a reason attached. Many of them, through verse 11, are close to the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope.

A meal at a ruler's table was a test. The food was deceptive because it came with strings: favor, obligation, a watching host. A young official was to keep his appetite, and his judgment, under control.

The picture of wealth growing wings and flying off like an eagle is one of the book's most memorable. Money can vanish in a moment.

Family land was a family's living and inheritance. Widows and orphans had no grown man to defend their claim at the town gate, so shifting the boundary stone at the edge of their field was an easy, quiet theft. Verse 11 answers that fear with a family word. A redeemer, go'el, was the nearest relative, bound to buy back a kinsman's land or rescue him from debt, as Boaz did in the book of Ruth. The orphan with no such relative has one after all. God himself takes up the case.
passages.later: The law gives the same warning: ‘You must not mistreat any widow or orphan. If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry’ (Exodus 22:22-23). And the psalm names God as the orphan's protector: ‘A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation’ (Psalm 68:5).
passages.asks: Wealth makes wings for itself. Ask how much of your strength you are spending to get rich, and whether you are wise enough to stop. And ask who around you has no one to defend them, since God says he is their Redeemer.

passages.t: Discipline, hope, and a father's joy
passages.happening:
‘Do not withhold discipline from a child; although you strike him with a rod, he will not die’ (verse 13). ‘Strike him with a rod, and you will deliver his soul from Sheol’ (verse 14).

The father's voice comes back. ‘My son, if your heart is wise, my own heart will indeed rejoice’ (verse 15). ‘Do not let your heart envy sinners, but always continue in the fear of the LORD’ (verse 17). ‘For surely there is a future, and your hope will not be cut off’ (verse 18).

‘Do not join those who drink too much wine or gorge themselves on meat’ (verse 20), for they come to poverty and rags (verse 21). ‘Listen to your father who gave you life, and do not despise your mother when she is old’ (verse 22). Buy truth and never sell it (verse 23). ‘May your father and mother be glad, and may she who gave you birth rejoice’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Discipline here is musar, which covers both teaching and correction. In verse 12 it is instruction the son must take to heart. In verse 13 it is the correction a parent must not hold back. For Proverbs, being teachable and being correctable are one virtue.

The rod reflects a world where physical correction of children was universal and where the greater fear was a child left with no correction at all, heading for an early death. Sheol is the realm of the dead.

Verses 17 and 18 meet a real temptation. When wrongdoers seem to do well, it is easy to envy them. The answer is not denial but hope: there is a future.

Verse 22 asks a son to honor his mother when she is old. In a world without pensions, aging parents depended on their children.
passages.later: The psalmist confessed the envy of verse 17: ‘For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked’ (Psalm 73:3). And Paul gives fathers a limit: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter teach that parents should strike their children, and does it promise that doing so will save them?

Verses 13 and 14 say that striking a child with a rod will not kill him, and will deliver his soul from Sheol, the realm of the dead. Faithful Christian parents read this in different ways.

Many read it as endorsing measured physical discipline, given in love and with self-control, never in anger and never to injure. Others note that the rod was a common picture for any firm correction, and they hold that the principle is loving, steady correction rather than a particular method, especially since physical punishment can so easily become abuse, which Scripture condemns. They point to the New Testament's word that fathers must not provoke their children (Ephesians 6:4; Colossians 3:21). This question divides faithful parents without dividing anyone from Christ, and these notes take no side.

Readers on every side agree that the passage is no license for harshness. Its point is that neglecting correction is itself a failure of love.

It also has to be read as a proverb. Proverbs describe how life usually goes under God, not guarantees. ‘He will not die’ is a pointed way of saying that correction does less harm than neglect. Deliverance from Sheol describes the ordinary fruit of a disciplined life: rescue from the early death that folly brings. It is not a formula that saves a child's soul, and it does not make parents solely responsible for a grown child's choices.

Nothing in these verses gives anyone a warrant to harm a child. Correction given in anger, or that injures a child, is not discipline at all.

Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The father's deepest wish is a son whose heart is wise. If you are a parent, ask what you most want for your children, and whether your correction serves that wish. And whoever you are, ask how you honor your father and mother now, especially if they are old.

passages.t: A heart given, and the drunkard's woe
passages.happening:
‘My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes delight in my ways’ (verse 26). The father warns again about the adulteress, who lies in wait like a robber (verses 27-28).

Then a poem about drink. “Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has contentions? Who has complaints? Who has needless wounds? Who has bloodshot eyes?” (verse 29). ‘Those who linger over wine, who go to taste mixed drinks’ (verse 30).

‘Do not gaze at wine while it is red, when it sparkles in the cup and goes down smoothly. In the end it bites like a snake and stings like a viper’ (verses 31-32). The drinker sees strange things and says twisted things, and he feels like someone lying on top of a ship's mast at sea (verses 33-34).

The poem ends with his own words. He has been beaten and felt nothing, and his first thought on waking is, “When can I wake up to search for another drink?” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the best-known poems in Proverbs. It opens with six quick questions and answers them in a single line. Then it moves from what attracts, wine red and sparkling in the cup, to what kills, the bite of a snake.

Mixed drinks were wine blended with spices or other ingredients, a practice known across the ancient world.

The poem ends by letting the drunkard speak for himself, and his last words are its sharpest point. He has been hurt and does not know it, and all he wants is another drink. The poem does not mock him. It shows how a habit becomes a trap.

If drinking has become hard to control, you do not have to face it alone. Tell someone you trust, and reach out to a doctor or a recovery group near you. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.later: Isaiah describes the same scene: ‘Woe to those who rise early in the morning in pursuit of strong drink, who linger into the evening, to be inflamed by wine’ (Isaiah 5:11). And Paul says, ‘Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit’ (Ephesians 5:18).
passages.asks: The father asks for his son's heart. Ask who or what has your heart right now. And ask honestly whether anything you drink, or anything else you reach for, has begun to have you instead of you having it.
